tldr: Evaluating the large foundation model GPT-6 Astra zero-shot on PhysLadder—16 household tasks stratified across three levels of contact complexity—revealed a 0% success rate on advanced manipulation (L3) requiring both contact reconfiguration and force regulation. This exposes a clear boundary where local physical progress fails to accumulate into overall task completion.
hero_caption: Overview of the 16 tasks proposed in PhysLadder and the tightly matched setup across simulation (purple) and the real world (orange). Tasks are hierarchically organized into three levels: geometric alignment (L1), force regulation under sustained contact (L2), and coordinated contact reconfiguration and force regulation (L3).
overview:
General foundation models like GPT-6 Astra are evolving rapidly in visual understanding and language reasoning, driving quick adoption in autonomous robotic manipulation. However, to be genuinely useful in real environments like homes and factories, robots must do more than simply pick and place objects; they must reliably handle contact-rich manipulation, where objects press, slide, or interlock against each other. Yet existing evaluation benchmarks only measure isolated task success rates, leaving us unable to systematically isolate which physical contact demands act as the model's bottleneck.

To address this, the authors built PhysLadder, a hierarchical benchmark that systematically categorizes tasks into three levels based on the complexity of their contact demands. Level 1 (L1) focuses on contact selection and geometric alignment, Level 2 (L2) involves force regulation while sustaining a single contact, and the most challenging Level 3 (L3) demands coordinated manipulation combining contact reconfiguration (such as regrasping) with force regulation. They also constructed a paired setup: a real-world bimanual robot platform and an Isaac Sim environment tightly calibrated in appearance, geometry, and contact mechanics, evaluating GPT-6 Astra zero-shot without task-specific demonstrations or training.

Experimental results showed a steep decline in real-world success rates as difficulty grew: 80.0% at L1, 47.6% at L2, and a total collapse to 0.0% at L3 (with an identical trend in simulation: 66.7% → 47.6% → 0.0%). While the model often made local physical progress—such as loosening a bottle cap slightly or pulling a drawer partway—it failed to sequence regrasp moves and regulate forces, never achieving final task completion. Furthermore, the success counts between the real robot and simulation matched exactly in 10 out of 16 tasks, demonstrating that calibrated simulation serves as a scalable, high-fidelity testbed for probing the physical limits of foundation models.
contributions: Proposed PhysLadder, a benchmark of 16 household manipulation tasks hierarchically organized across three levels (L1–L3) along two axes: contact configuration and force regulation.

Constructed an Isaac Sim environment meticulously matched to the real platform in appearance, geometry, mass, friction, and deformation characteristics, providing a reproducible sim-to-real evaluation testbed.

Conducted zero-shot evaluations of the cutting-edge foundation model GPT-6 Astra, empirically uncovering a hard boundary in physical manipulation ability with a 0% success rate on L3 tasks requiring simultaneous contact reconfiguration and force regulation.

Identified four interconnected interaction bottlenecks—spatial reasoning, contact selection, force regulation, and coordination—that prevent local physical progress from translating into task completion.

sections.heading: Why do we need a hierarchy for contact-rich manipulation?
sections.summary: While applying foundation models to robotics is advancing quickly, reliably executing contact-rich manipulation remains a challenge. The authors developed PhysLadder, a benchmark organizing 16 tasks into three levels based on contact configuration and force regulation demands, aiming to uncover the physical boundaries of GPT-6 Astra in both sim and real environments.
sections.details:
Frontier models such as GPT-6 Astra demonstrate remarkable capabilities in instruction following and high-level task planning. However, operating robots in homes and factories requires contact-rich manipulation: finding appropriate contact points, regulating applied forces, and coordinating contact adjustments like regrasp maneuvers as the task unfolds. Many conventional benchmarks only track overall end-to-end success rates, making it impossible to diagnose where models stumble along the spectrum of physical interactions.

To solve this, the authors introduce PhysLadder. It frames physical contact requirements along two cumulative axes:
- Contact Configuration: Where and how to establish contact with or grasp objects and tools, and whether mid-task contact switching (reconfiguration) is needed.
- Force Regulation: Managing forces and torques through contact surfaces to overcome friction or resistance, maintain steady pressure, or prevent fragile objects from deforming.

These two axes define three hierarchical levels: L1 (contact selection and geometric alignment), L2 (force regulation within sustained contact), and L3 (coordinated contact reconfiguration and force regulation). They paired a real-world setup with an Isaac Sim simulation carefully matched both physically and visually. Evaluating GPT-6 Astra zero-shot revealed a sharp drop in real-world success from 80.0% at L1 to 47.6% at L2, and down to 0.0% at L3, with almost identical trends in simulation. This highlighted that while the model can produce local motions, it fails to accumulate them into full task completion.

sections.heading: Tracing embodied evaluation and sim-to-real matching in foundation models
sections.summary: Embodied evaluation of foundation models has moved from high-level reasoning to closed-loop control, yet granular analysis of physical contact remains underdeveloped. This work systematizes contact demands that existing benchmarks missed, leveraging tight sim-to-real matching to capture the physical limits of models.
sections.details:
### 2.1 Embodied Evaluation of General Foundation Models
Evaluating whether foundation models can interpret visual and language instructions to act under environmental feedback (e.g., EmbodiedEval, EmbodiedBench) has grown rapidly. Even frontier models like GPT-6 Astra, while showcasing strong semantic comprehension, still struggle with precision manipulation, dynamic control, and bimanual coordination. A benchmark specifically designed to measure the gap between high-level understanding and reliable physical manipulation was sorely needed.

### 2.2 Contact-Rich Manipulation Benchmarks
Prior benchmarks have focused on contact, such as assembly or articulated object manipulation. However, they were often tied to narrow task categories (like peg insertion or furniture assembly) rather than systematically deconstructing the difficulty of contact itself. PhysLadder stands out by organizing tasks not by domain or step count, but around shared physical demands: contact configuration and force regulation.

### 2.3 Physical and Visual Matching in Sim-to-Real Evaluation
Evaluating a model's contact capabilities in simulation requires close alignment with the real world in both visual appearance and contact dynamics. Incorporating modern scene reconstruction and deformable-body simulation to empirically verify that behaviors and failure modes match across sim and real is a foundational pillar of this research.

sections.heading: The design philosophy behind PhysLadder's 3-level contact hierarchy
sections.summary: PhysLadder organizes 16 household manipulation tasks into levels L1 through L3 based on physical interaction demands. Critically, levels are determined by initial conditions and constraints rather than task names alone, separating local physical progress (effective contact) from overall task success.
sections.details:
### 3.1 Core Principles of the Hierarchical Design
PhysLadder's levels are structured along two cumulative axes:
- **L1: Contact Selection & Geometric Alignment**
Tasks that require grasping an object correctly and aligning it to a target position and orientation. These involve free-space transport and geometric matching without needing to overcome substantial resistance or finely tune applied force (e.g., placing a marker in a cup, aligning a charger with a socket).
- **L2: Force Regulation within Sustained Contact**
Tasks where contact (a grasp or a tool press) is maintained while forces are regulated to overcome friction or resistance, or to prevent damage and excessive deformation (e.g., pushing and pulling a drawer, wiping a whiteboard, grasping a soft jelly). No regrasp is required mid-task.
- **L3: Coordinated Contact Reconfiguration & Force Regulation**
Tasks that cannot be finished in a single grasp posture. The robot must release and re-establish contact (regrasping) while regulating forces and preventing state slip to continue the task (e.g., repeatedly twisting off a bottle cap, sweeping scattered blocks into a dustpan).

Crucially, a task's level is determined by its initial state and constraints (task version) rather than its name. For instance, sweeping blocks clustered directly in front of a dustpan is an L2 task because one sweep suffices; if the blocks are scattered, requiring repeated contact switches, it becomes an L3 task.

### 3.2 16 Tasks and Success Criteria
The benchmark comprises 5 tasks in L1, 7 in L2, and 4 in L3. It covers rigid objects, deformable items like an orange and a jelly, and articulated or threaded mechanisms like drawers and bolts. In addition to final success (such as a cap being fully removed and lifted to a target height), the benchmark defines an intermediate diagnostic metric called "effective contact" to track whether force or torque was successfully transmitted, allowing fine-grained tracking of local progress.

sections.heading: How closely were simulation and reality matched?
sections.summary: The real-world platform uses two 6-DoF ARX R5 arms and three RGB cameras, mirrored inside Isaac Sim across both visuals and mechanics. Beyond measuring masses and geometries, friction and deformable dynamics were calibrated directly against real-world observations.
sections.details:
### 4.1 Real-World Setup
The real environment features two ARX R5 robot arms (6-DoF each, with 2-finger parallel grippers) clamped to a tabletop. This enables both single-arm tasks and bimanual coordination, such as stabilizing an object with one hand while manipulating it with the other. The vision system uses three RGB cameras: one global overhead camera (Orbbec Gemini Pro) and two wrist-mounted cameras (Orbbec Gemini 305). The robot has no wrist force/torque sensors; the model receives only RGB images. Force regulation must therefore be achieved indirectly via end-effector displacement and gripper width commands.

### 4.2 Simulation Environment and Asset Creation
The authors built the simulation in NVIDIA Isaac Sim. Using automated segmentation and 3D reconstruction from real video, they replicated the workspace, including table textures and background walls. Across 21 assets, exact real-world dimensions and visual appearance were reproduced, faithfully modeling kinematic joints like drawer slides and screw threads. For soft objects like jelly and orange, Finite Element Method (FEM) models were implemented to reproduce elastic deformation under gripper pressure. For the whiteboard wiping task, custom logic clears ink based on normal contact force and travel distance.

### 4.3 Physical and Visual Matching
To close the sim-to-real gap, four aspects were tightly calibrated:
- Workspace Layout: Table dimensions, initial object poses, and initial bolt thread engagements were strictly matched.
- Contact Response: The jelly's mass (measured at 26.4 g) was matched, and Young's modulus was tuned by comparing deformation profiles against real video footage.
- Robot Kinematics: Using open-source ARX R5 models, joint limits, kinematic trees, and wrist camera relative offsets were aligned.
- Camera Views: Field of view and camera placements were adjusted using real footage as reference to align both wrist and third-person viewpoints.

sections.heading: Evaluating GPT-6 Astra: Closed-loop execution and protocol
sections.summary: GPT-6 Astra was evaluated zero-shot within a Codex execution runtime using the 'xhigh' reasoning effort setting, without task-specific demonstrations. The model receives three RGB views and proprioception, outputs target end-effector poses in a closed loop, and performs self-verification toward task completion.
sections.details:
### 5.1 Model Settings and Zero-Shot Definition
The evaluated model is GPT-6 Astra with reasoning effort set to 'xhigh', running within the Codex execution environment. The evaluation is strictly zero-shot: no task-specific trajectory demonstrations, prior success examples, or strategic hints are provided. The model makes autonomous decisions relying solely on runtime RGB images, proprioception (joint states and gripper widths), and previous action history.

### 5.2 Inputs and the Closed-Loop Execution Loop
At each decision step, the model receives:
- Task instructions and interface definitions: Natural language goals, constraints, coordinate frame definitions, and available tools. On the real robot, this is delivered via a task-agnostic system prompt called 'Basic Skills', which explains frame conventions and camera-arm correspondences.
- Observations: Three RGB images (one global and two wrist views), current end-effector poses, and execution feedback from the previous action. No depth maps or F/T sensor values are provided.

Based on these inputs, the model outputs the next target end-effector pose and gripper width. In simulation, the cuRobo planner generates collision-free trajectories; on the real robot, commands are executed through a control service with safety limits. After moving, the model inspects new images to verify whether the intended contact occurred, deciding the next action or declaring task completion.

### 5.3 Evaluation Protocol and Success Criteria
Each task is evaluated across 3 trials per environment. In simulation, an independent evaluation program automatically checks geometric conditions and contact states (up to 150 model calls or 5 hours). In the real world, human evaluators score trials using execution logs and video recordings. A trial is marked as a failure if the model deems the task impossible and aborts, if arm singularities or collisions trigger safety stops, or if human intervention is required.

sections.heading: Astra's current frontier: Why did L3 success drop to 0%?
sections.summary: Astra achieved 80.0% success at L1, 47.6% at L2, and 0.0% at L3 on the real robot, with nearly identical trends in simulation. While the model showed local progress like twisting a cap, four compounding bottlenecks—spatial reasoning, contact selection, force regulation, and coordination—blocked overall task completion.
sections.details:
### 6.1 Performance Drop Across Interaction Levels
Across all 16 tasks, average success was 45.8% in the real world and 41.7% in simulation. As shown in Table 2, the drop in performance with increasing interaction level is striking:
- **L1 (Geometric Alignment)**: 80.0% Real, 66.7% Sim. Tasks like marker insertion and charger alignment succeeded reliably. However, in 'Hat Hanging'—which requires complex 3D spatial reasoning to align the opening with an angled hook after lifting—the model failed every trial in both environments.
- **L2 (Force Regulation in Sustained Contact)**: 47.6% Real, 47.6% Sim. In tasks maintaining contact against resistance, such as drawer pulling or book extraction, success and failure split evenly.
- **L3 (Coordinated Contact Reconfiguration & Force Regulation)**: 0.0% Real, 0.0% Sim. Across all four tasks—bottle un-capping, bolt un-screwing, book re-orienting, and block sweeping—the model failed to achieve a single complete success.

### 6.2 Remarkable Sim-to-Real Correlation
Crucially, 10 out of 16 tasks had identical success counts (out of 3 trials) between real and sim environments, while the remaining 6 differed by only a single trial. Furthermore, intermediate behaviors and failure modes (such as failing to lift jelly due to slipping, or dropping a cap mid-twist) matched closely across both environments. This confirms that a carefully calibrated simulation provides a reliable testbed for evaluating the physical boundaries of foundation models.

### 6.3 Sensitivity to Initial Conditions
Task difficulty is heavily sensitive to initial layouts. In the block sweeping task, when blocks were clustered near the dustpan opening (an L2 configuration), a short local sweep succeeded. However, when three blocks were scattered across the table (an L3 configuration), the robot had to repeatedly adjust its approach angle, reposition the broom, and balance sweeping forces, causing the model to fail completely.

### 6.4 Four Interaction Bottlenecks
Detailed failure log analysis identified four core bottlenecks:
1. Spatial Reasoning & Precision: Detecting an object's position does not guarantee accurate relative orientation alignment (e.g., hat hanging, charger insertion).
2. Contact Configuration Selection & Establishment: Failing to choose grasp poses that transmit stable forces (e.g., shallow edge grasps on caps, or slipping off jelly to avoid crushing it).
3. Force Regulation Limits: Inability to balance push-pull forces after contact (e.g., pressing too hard on adjacent books during extraction, or failing to push drawers flush).
4. Coordination Failure in Contact Reconfiguration: Inability to preserve physical state across regrasp cycles, leading to dropped caps after partial rotations.
In short, while GPT-6 Astra can make local progress like loosening a cap, its key weakness is failing to accumulate that progress toward the final goal.

sections.heading: Conclusions and the path toward Physical AI
sections.summary: Evaluating GPT-6 Astra on PhysLadder reveals that while foundation models handle geometric placement well, sustained force regulation and dynamic contact switching remain major hurdles. Proving that calibrated simulation mirrors real-world physical bottlenecks provides a roadmap for advancing embodied intelligence.
sections.details:
This work introduced PhysLadder, a hierarchical benchmark for contact-rich robotic manipulation, and thoroughly evaluated GPT-6 Astra zero-shot in both real-world and simulated environments. The key takeaways include:
- While Astra excels at semantic understanding and simple pick-and-place tasks, its performance falls sharply as physical contact demands rise, collapsing to 0% on L3 tasks combining contact reconfiguration and force regulation.
- The root failure is the inability to accumulate local physical progress into task completion, constrained by bottlenecks in spatial reasoning, contact selection, force regulation, and temporal coordination.
- A simulation environment carefully calibrated in appearance and contact mechanics accurately mirrors both task outcomes and intermediate failure patterns observed on physical hardware.

For general-purpose robots to achieve genuine Physical Intelligence, future breakthroughs must look beyond high-level task planning and master continuous force regulation while dynamically updating contact states.

sections.heading: Appendix: Implementation details and evaluation protocols
sections.summary: The appendix details task specifications, Isaac Sim physical parameters (such as FEM models and ink wiping logic), and the structure of the Basic Skills prompts used within the Codex runtime.
sections.details:
### A Task Specifications and Success Criteria
Appendix A defines initial setups, objectives, geometric tolerances, and process constraints for all 16 tasks. For example, 'L1-02: Charger Alignment' does not require socket insertion, defining success as having both pins aligned directly in front of the holes. For the jelly task, avoiding any surface cuts or damage is a strict requirement.

### B Technical Details of Sim-to-Real Implementation
- Real Robot Platform (B.1): Arm control runs over CAN bus communication. Wrist camera feeds stream at $848\times 480$ (15 fps), and the global camera runs at $640\times 480$ (30 fps), delivered to the model as JPEG snapshots upon tool calls.
- Simulation Platform (B.2): Running on Isaac Sim 5.1.0, real-time collision-free trajectories are generated using cuRobo. Contact dynamics are captured using FEM models for jelly elasticity and a custom ink-clearing algorithm where whiteboard ink erases proportional to normal contact force multiplied by travel distance.

### C Evaluation Protocol and Basic Skills
The 'Basic Skills' prompt used in real-world trials is a task-agnostic system prompt describing arm assignments, camera-to-arm spatial relationships, gripper width units, and safe incremental motion rules. It contains no task-specific heuristics, serving purely as a general user manual for operating the robotic embodiment.

takeaways: Evaluating foundation models along two physical axes—contact reconfiguration and force regulation—is far more diagnostic than sorting by task names or step counts.
Even frontier models like GPT-6 Astra struggle zero-shot on L3 tasks requiring regrasp cycles and sustained force regulation (0% success), despite being able to produce local physical motion.
When appearance, geometry, mass, friction, and elasticity are calibrated against real measurements, Isaac Sim faithfully reproduces physical interaction failures seen on real hardware.
High-level vision-language reasoning alone cannot prevent physical contact failures, highlighting an urgent need for closed-loop policies integrating tactile and force feedback.
limitations: Due to the high cost of real-world trials and safety stop interventions, each task was evaluated across only 3 trials, resulting in a small sample size.

Tight sim-to-real correlation was demonstrated exclusively on GPT-6 Astra; whether this correspondence holds for other foundation models, reinforcement learning, or imitation learning policies remains untested.
The robot end-effectors lacked tactile or wrist force/torque sensors, leaving it partially ambiguous whether failures stem from model reasoning limits or the absence of contact sensing modalities.
